extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemaking staff, policymakers, and administrative law practitioners responsible for managing public comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on policy, technical, and procedural approaches for identifying, handling, and making use of mass, malattributed, and computer-generated public comments in administrative rulemaking. Covers detection heuristics, authentication tradeoffs, use of NLP/summarization, and innovations for participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: User notice as deterrence for malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A user notice that warns that malattributed comments could be a federal crime may serve as part of a deterrence strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes uncertainty about whether users will notice such a warning among many policy paragraphs and doubts about its effectiveness against large-scale operations. It may discourage some individual submitters but is unlikely to affect organized mass operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency protocols for addressing suspected malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt protocols for deciding how to treat comments suspected or discovered to be malattributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should address whether an agency should strive to resolve a question about a comment’s provenance or merely flag the potential issue. If criminal action is considered, agencies may need staff available to assist investigations or prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication technologies available to agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Common techniques exist to authenticate users — e.g., secure login, two-factor authentication, biometric authentication, security questions, verifying names against a database, or an additional affirmative click to acknowledge terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although technically straightforward in many contexts, agencies currently lack the identity-authentication infrastructure akin to driver’s license issuance or commercial transaction authentication. Adoption must consider resource costs and policy tradeoffs (notably anonymity).

rubrics_metrics.name: CAPTCHA / reCAPTCHA as a human-vs-bot mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPTCHA functions as a Turing Test to distinguish humans from bots; reCAPTCHA v3 uses risk analysis algorithms and assigns risk scores without human interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAPTCHA provides a "speed bump" and is intended to “improve[] the integrity of the commenting process,” but older CAPTCHAs can be defeated and newer approaches (reCAPTCHA v3) rely on risk scoring. Limitations include evolving attacker capabilities and potential false positives/negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verified comment API for authorized mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov includes a comment API that allows authorized entities to post mass comment campaigns if verified by GSA using a commercial identity validation service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The API aims to assure that entities 'are who they say they are' but does not verify the identities of individual commenters. Useful for organizational actors but does not address individual-level authentication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between authentication and anonymous comments policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing front-end authentication for commenters would be in tension with existing agency policies permitting anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must balance the desire to authenticate identities against procedural policies and rights to submit anonymously; this tension affects feasibility and acceptability of authentication measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA definitions and scope regarding who may comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires agencies to provide an opportunity to comment to 'interested persons' and defines 'person' broadly to include individuals, partnerships, corporations, associations, or public or private organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'person' is not limited to natural persons and courts have read the term capaciously, computer-generated comments may fall within this broad definition (and, in any event, a person sets a computer-generated comment in motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to consider significant issues regardless of comment origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to respond to significant issues raised in comments and indicated commitment to reviewing comments regardless of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency staff emphasized that substance matters more than source or volume; they would not exclude a comment solely because it was computer-generated, but would assess whether it raises significant issues requiring consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court considerations regarding reliability/authenticity in challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: If litigation arises claiming inadequate consideration of computer-generated comments, courts may evaluate reliability or authenticity of such comments when deciding whether a suit should proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report suggests courts might use analogies to evidentiary standards (relevance, reliability, authenticity) or other equitable powers consistent with the APA; proponents of evidence would need to demonstrate those qualities if challenging agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical difficulty of distinguishing computer-generated from human comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Advances in text generation allow bots to mimic human speech, making it difficult to distinguish computer-generated comments from human submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An experiment found respondents (competent at spotting bots) correctly classified less than half of comments and identified computer-generated comments less than one-third of the time — indicating consistent sorting is non-trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual heuristics indicating computer-generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Search-and-replace algorithms and repetition of particular phrases, brevity, repeated words, incorrect grammar, or nonsensical sentiment may indicate computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of net neutrality comments found recurring sentence fragments and permutations consistent with automated search-and-replace; shorter comments reduce 'tells' that reveal non-human authorship, while longer comments provide more opportunities for indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and submission-pattern indicators (mass/automated campaigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns such as large numbers of comments submitted at the exact same second, constant near-constant submission rates punctuated by interludes, or on-off cycles suggest automated bot activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FCC analysis discovered many instances of such timing clusters (e.g., >75,000 comments at the same second), and cycles consistent with bots turning on/off at intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadata indicators: email and field consistency anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition in email addresses, domains that cannot receive messages, many submissions from identical geographic sources, unusually complete and uniform name/address/email fields, and few requests for confirmation of receipt can indicate algorithmic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include millions from one-off email producers and hundreds of thousands from the same address in Russia; human-filled metadata typically shows variability and omissions, while bot-generated metadata can be highly uniform and complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of de-duplication software to manage mass and computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies commonly use de-duplication tools to address mass comments; these tools can reduce the impact of computer-generated comments by identifying unique content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency staff often perceive computer-generated comments as a de-duplication task; deduping software helps identify the unique substantive content among many similar submissions, reducing the need for separate bot-detection efforts in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening methods must preserve obligation to consider unique substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies that identify or filter computer-generated comments must not exclude ordinary comments that raise unique significant issues; screening must account for agencies' duty to consider and respond to significant comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authentication or detection tools exclude comments that raise new significant issues, agencies may fail to meet legal obligations; detection systems must be calibrated to avoid false negatives on important content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor technology impacts on perceived legitimacy and processing capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should monitor whether technologies that enable mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments threaten the perceived legitimacy of notice-and-comment and the ability of agency officials to make sense of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although current perceptions downplay some threats, future developments might undermine legitimacy or thoughtful consideration; ongoing monitoring and adaptation are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NLP and summarization technologies to enhance comment review
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural language processing (NLP) techniques can summarize and sort comments, identify parts of comments relevant to rule-writers, and extract legal, technical, or operational information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include topic modeling, automated summarization, readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid), LIWC, plagiarism detection, sentiment analysis, and word embeddings. These tools can help surface 'needle-in-the-haystack' issues and synthesize large volumes for rulewriters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine machine summarization with human oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Automation is often most effective when paired with human review to overcome automation biases and validate outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: journalists used combined methods to analyze the Paradise Papers; the State Department used a text-mining vendor and public proofing for passport-feedback summaries. Challenges include domain-specific language requiring retraining of models; human oversight can verify reliability and improve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit consideration for deploying advanced NLP in high-volume rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Investment in advanced NLP and retraining models may be justified for rulemakings likely to receive large numbers of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should weigh the upfront costs and retraining needs against potential efficiency and analytic gains in high-volume proceedings; human oversight can mitigate risks and legal uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/regulatory uncertainty may slow adoption of new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency staff expressed concern that legal obligations to review and respond to comments create uncertainty about reliance on machine tools, which may impede innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal uncertainty could cause agencies to innovate slowly or avoid adopting NLP/summarization technologies without clear policy or guidance on how to meet statutory obligations while using automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize-backed challenges require transparent, specific evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize-backed challenges (Challenge.gov) force agencies to articulate exactly what information they need and to provide transparent, specific criteria for evaluating public submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With a decade of experience, prize-backed challenges offer insights into how to improve participation; clear, public criteria improve legitimacy and make submissions comparable and evaluable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sourcing and collaborative annotation to elicit and surface expert input
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies can use online collaborative drafting and annotation platforms to obtain detailed feedback from experts and make one another’s feedback visible (e.g., Hypothes.is used by German government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborative annotation facilitates deeper expert engagement than isolated comments, enabling experts to annotate draft rules and see each other's feedback; suitable for domain-specific, technical rulemaking and expert sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mini-publics (citizen juries/assemblies) to improve representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Random samples of members of the public (mini-publics) assembled via technology can provide more legitimate and diverse participation than open comment alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tech makes assembling representative samples easier; mini-publics (citizen juries or assemblies) can be used to weigh in on governance processes and to engage underrepresented communities, improving legitimacy of input.
